tip: To retire is 'prendre sa retraite' – literally take one's retirement. 'Il a pris sa retraite' = he retired.
Slip 'de' before the adjective: 'quelque chose de bizarre', literally something OF strange. Same with 'quelqu'un de gentil', 'rien de neuf'.
'Faire connaissance' – literally make acquaintance – is how you say you first met someone. 'Nous avons fait connaissance' = we met.
You're kind 'avec' someone, not 'to' them: 'gentilles avec nous' = kind to us. French uses with where English uses to.
The object pronoun normally comes before the verb: 'me voir' = to see me, literally 'me to-see'. Little words like 'me' sit in front, not after.
Before a plural adjective, 'des' shrinks to 'de': 'de nouveaux plats', not 'des nouveaux plats'. Compare 'de beaux jardins'.
Repeated actions in the past use imparfait. 'Chaque matin' signals a habit.
Mental states in the past usually use imparfait: 'je pensais', 'je croyais', 'je savais'.
'Attendre' already means wait FOR – no extra word needed: 'attendions le bus' = waited for the bus. Adding 'pour' would be wrong.
A sunset is a 'coucher de soleil' – literally the sun's lying-down. Sunrise flips it: 'lever de soleil', the sun getting up.
'Ten-page' becomes 'de dix pages' after the noun: 'un rapport de dix pages'. French hangs the measurement off the noun with 'de'.
To hear from someone is 'avoir des nouvelles de' – literally have news of. 'Des nouvelles de Pierre' = word from Pierre.
Before doing something, use 'avant de' + the plain verb: 'avant de sortir' = before going out, literally before to-go-out.
'The same as' is 'la même... que': 'la même chose que moi' = the same thing as me. And it's 'moi', the stressed form, never 'je'.
'Chez' means at someone's place or office: 'chez le dentiste' = at the dentist's. Use 'chez' with people, not 'à'.
'Mettre' also means 'to take (time)': 'j'ai mis deux heures' = it took me two hours. Very common usage.
You don't 'have' a dream in French, you make one: 'j'ai fait un rêve' = I had a dream. It's 'faire', not 'avoir', with 'rêve'.
'Il y avait' (there was or there were) uses imparfait to describe past situations.
'Collège' is middle school, not college – a classic false friend. 'Au collège' means roughly ages 11 to 15. University is 'la fac'.
Colours land after the noun, but age words go before: 'un vieux camion bleu' = an old blue truck. 'Vieux' leads, 'bleu' trails.
'Avoir envie de' means to feel like, not to envy: 'j'ai eu envie de partir' = I felt like leaving. French 'has' the urge.
Imparfait for the ongoing action ('lisais'), passé composé for the interruption ('a sonné').
'Avoir l'habitude de' = to be used to, literally 'to have the habit of': 'nous avions l'habitude de dîner' = we usually had dinner.
Imparfait sets the scene ('marchais'), passé composé introduces a new event ('ai vu').
To love something in general, French adds 'les': 'adorions les vacances' = loved vacations. English drops the article here; French never does.
Two pronouns stack before the verb: 'me l'a dit' = said it to me ('le' shrinks before the vowel). Order: 'me/te/se/nous/vous' before 'le/la/les'.
With 'depuis', French stays in the present for something still true: 'nous le connaissons depuis l'enfance' = we've known him since childhood.
'Tous les dimanches' (every Sunday) is a clear habit marker → imparfait is the right tense.
'Jouer à' is for games and sports: 'jouaient aux cartes' = played cards ('à' + 'les' = 'aux'). Instruments switch to 'jouer de'.
'Se souvenir' needs both a reflexive pronoun and 'de': 'te souvenais de cette chanson' = remembered this song. The 'de' is not optional.
